title: The Physical Limits of Reactive Oxygen Species
content: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are widely regarded as principal mediators of oxidative stress, ageing and disease. Yet the extent to which ROS can accumulate in living systems is constrained by fundamental principles of cellular chemistry. Oxygen availability, respiratory efficiency and antioxidant removal collectively impose strict limits on ROS production and persistence, allowing for localised signalling rather than diffuse oxidant production. We argue that many assumptions of the modern oxidative stress paradigm derive from radiation chemistry and toxicology, where oxidant fluxes are substantially higher than those typically encountered in biology. Consistent with this view, broad antioxidant interventions have repeatedly failed to provide the predicted therapeutic benefit. Rather than denying a role for ROS, here we examine the conditions under which ROS chemistry is quantitatively plausible and identifies biological contexts where ROS can genuinely become primary cellular oxidants. We propose that ROS-dependent mechanisms should be evaluated using the same standards applied to any other signalling molecule: demonstrable production, biologically plausible concentrations, defined targets, and quantitative consistency with the cellular environment.
